title: Thanksgiving
hookLine: in North America, a harvest thanks at the table

cards: The ship has been driven by a storm for fourteen days. No sun, no stars. The cargo has gone over the side.
The sailors have just been caught trying to slip away in the lifeboat. It's the dark before dawn, and nobody has eaten properly since the storm began.

Then a prisoner, a tentmaker called Paul, takes a loaf and does something ordinary. He says grace. A strange place to begin a day about Thanksgiving, North America's harvest meal with thanks at the table.

teach.h: PAUL SAYS GRACE IN A STORM.
teach.b: In Acts, in the King James words, Paul urges them all to eat, and then "he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all: and when he had broken it, he began to eat."
The storm isn't over; the ship hasn't reached land. He gives thanks in the middle, in front of terrified people, and then: "Then were they all of good cheer, and they also took some meat."
One person's grace turned into everyone's breakfast. That grace has a pattern behind it.

teach.h: JESUS TOOK THE LOAVES AND GAVE THANKS.
teach.b: In Mark, with a hungry crowd in the wilderness, Jesus takes the loaves, gives thanks, breaks them, and gives them to his disciples to set before the people.
In Luke, two friends at Emmaus only recognize the risen Jesus when he takes bread, blesses it and breaks it. More than once, the meal begins with thanks.
A letter in Paul's name says: "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." Creature there means every created thing. The potatoes count.
And to the church at Thessalonica, Paul wrote: "In every thing give thanks." Not for every thing, some readers point out. In every thing.

At a Thanksgiving table, grace changes from house to house: a psalm, "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever," a grandmother's grace, or just hands held for a moment.
The shape is the ship's: stop, give thanks out loud, then eat together.

how: Some Christian families in the United States and Canada say grace before the Thanksgiving meal, sometimes holding hands, and some churches hold a Thanksgiving service or gather food for neighbors in need.

games.q: you're Paul. fourteen days of storm, almost nobody has eaten, frightened sailors all around you. it's nearly dawn. what do you do?
o: pray loudly for the sea to go calm.
take bread, give thanks in front of everyone, and eat.
tell everyone to save the last food for later.
games.why: he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all, and began to eat. then were they all of good cheer.

practice: Think of your next meal, and of one thing in your life still unsettled, a storm still going; don't try to solve it, just let it be there. Then choose a few plain words of thanks to say before that meal anyway.
If you pray, use a grace your family knows, or the psalm's line, O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good; if not, just choose the words, and the breath you'll pause for.

wordCard.voice: Thanksgiving. In North America, a harvest meal with thanks at the table. In the Bible, giving thanks in every thing, even in a storm.

orig.note: Greek, Mark 8:6: having given thanks, before Jesus broke the loaves and gave them to his disciples.
